title: The AI Researcher
answer: Ten areas where artificial intelligence is changing research and teaching: literature review, citation mapping, quantitative and qualitative analysis, grants, writing and peer review, course design, research data, the laboratory, and the integrity rules that govern all of it.

sections.body: Artificial intelligence in research and teaching is now a set of practical tools for finding, reading, organising, analysing, writing, and assessing scholarly work. Literature review systems help search and screen papers, citation mapping tools trace how ideas connect, and quantitative and qualitative analysis tools assist with coding, statistics, and pattern finding. Grant offices use AI to draft sections, check compliance, and match calls, while journals and authors use it for writing support, reviewer matching, and integrity screening. Course design tools help build syllabi, questions, and feedback loops, and laboratory systems use automation and simulation to plan experiments and manage instruments. Research data work uses AI for metadata, repository search, and reproducibility checks, and governance pages set the rules for disclosure, bias, privacy, and authorship. The site's library holds 135 research papers and 12,646 extracted claims, which shows the scale of evidence being organised in this area.
sections.heading: What this covers

sections.body: Some parts are mature, especially search, citation graph exploration, statistical modelling, and routine data cleaning, where AI is a faster assistant rather than an autonomous scholar. Literature screening and citation mapping still miss context, struggle with work in languages other than English, and can amplify gaps in the record. Qualitative analysis tools can suggest codes and themes, but interpretation remains contested and depends on human judgement, positionality, and domain knowledge. Grant and peer review uses raise clear risks around confidentiality, bias, and ghostwriting, and many institutions are still writing policies for disclosure and accountability. Laboratory automation works well for narrow, well instrumented tasks, but open ended discovery, wet lab improvisation, and cross domain reasoning remain hard. The honest limit is that AI can accelerate parts of the research cycle, yet it cannot guarantee truth, reproduce a finding by itself, or replace the ethical responsibility of researchers and teachers.
sections.heading: Where the work stands

sections.body: The pages begin with Literature Review and Evidence Synthesis and Citation Mapping and Discovery, which cover how AI helps find, screen, and connect prior work. Quantitative Analysis and Reproducible Work and Qualitative Analysis and Mixed Methods then show how AI enters data analysis, from statistics and code to coding and theme building. Grant Proposals and Funding and Academic Writing and Peer Review address the production and evaluation of scholarly text, including funding searches, drafting, reviewer support, and integrity checks. Course Design and Teaching and Research Data and Repositories extend the same concerns into classrooms and data infrastructure, where AI supports learning design, metadata, storage, and reuse. Laboratory Automation and Simulation covers instrument control, experiment planning, and simulated environments, while Governance, Ethics and Research Integrity sits across all of them as the rules for disclosure, bias, privacy, authorship, and misconduct. A reader can go to the first pair for discovery, the middle pages for analysis and writing, the later pages for teaching and data, and the final page for the norms that bind the rest.
